title: The Mathematics of Weight-Space Programming: Behavioral Optimality, Finite Preservation, and Transformers

target_networks.name: fifteen small two-block pre-LayerNorm transformers (residual width 32, vocabulary 8)

domain: theory of selective weight editing (model editing, constrained optimization)
tasks_benchmarks: controlled modular/selection tasks on 4,096 prefixes (480 target-donor pairs, 3,840 edits)

headline_result.text: Behavioral optimization cut median edit norms by 33-40% on small transformers, and on GPT-2 finite interval constraints raised held-out neighbor retention by 21.1 and 19.4 points over a matched exact-moment control at 100% efficacy, with lower paraphrase success and higher test loss.
headline_result.quote: Against a matched exact-moment control, finite interval constraints improve held-out neighbor retention by 21.1 and 19.4 percentage points at 100% target success, with reduced paraphrase success and increased test loss.

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: 5 seeds per controlled task family; 2 pretrained checkpoints x 128 cases

key_claims.claim: The paper analyses the weight-editing problem with explicit numerical algorithms and states that it does not test the MIT claim that LLMs can autonomously write weights.
key_claims.quote: Here we analyze the editing problem itself; the numerical editors below are explicit algorithms, not tests of that autonomous capability.

key_claims.claim: For the last transformer MLP, the globally minimum-cost single-target edit under module-output protection reduces to a strictly convex scalar optimization.
key_claims.quote: and reduce the globally nearest feasible residual to a strictly convex scalar optimization. This yields a globally minimum-cost single-target edit under fixed-key module-output protection.

key_claims.claim: In the controlled study, behavioral optimization reduced median edit norms by 40.0%, 33.2% and 34.0% versus a centered-donor control, but these gains rely on a small-vocabulary readout nullspace.
key_claims.quote: The gains exploit this small-vocabulary nullspace; they do not predict complete-logit gains for injective language-model heads.

key_claims.claim: On GPT-2 124M, Interval-QP reached 59.77% neighbor retention versus 38.67% for exact-moment and 30.16% for a ROME-style final-layer edit, all at 100% efficacy.
Arithmetic cost of direct-access edits says nothing about whether an LLM can execute the editor natively.
key_claims.quote: These arithmetic costs do not establish that an LLM reads or executes the editor natively.

limitations_stated.text: Earlier-layer certificates, multi-token rewrites, pretrained sequential edits and multi-billion-parameter models are outside the evidence.
limitations_stated.quote: General earlier-layer margin certificates, multi-token rewrites, pretrained sequential edits, linguistic-family coverage, and multi- billion-parameter models remain beyond this evidence.

limitations_stated.text: Retention outside the stated constraints is empirical, and full greedy continuations are preserved far less often than first tokens.
limitations_stated.quote: Interval-QP retains 95.7% of unrelated first tokens but only 72.3% of full eight-token greedy continuations; exact-moment retains 96.9% and 74.2%.

limitations_stated.text: Numerical audits are floating-point checks, not interval-arithmetic proofs.
limitations_stated.quote: These are floating-point checks, not interval-arithmetic proofs.

notes_for_review: A mathematical treatment of selective weight editing (feasibility, minimum edit cost, margin-preserving intervals, dual refusal witnesses) motivated by the MIT blog, with no LLM in the loop; all edits are computed by closed-form or convex solvers. Experiments are small but carefully controlled (fixed splits, full-forward checks, paired bootstrap on CounterFact) and compare against ROME/AlphaEdit-style final-layer adaptations. Useful to the review as a formal baseline for what a mechanical editor can guarantee, and for the explicit statement that edit arithmetic does not show an LLM can do it natively.
